title: Hoisting
body:
```js 
let s = sum(3,4);

function sum(a,b) {
	return a+b
}
//Function declaration are hoisted to the top. 
```
---

The JS engine reads the whole scope before running any of it, so **function declarations exist
from the first line of the scope**, whatever line they were written on. That is why the call
above works.

What is *not* hoisted usefully:

```js
console.log(a);   // undefined  <- var is hoisted, its assignment is not
var a = 3;

console.log(b);   // ReferenceError
let b = 3;        // let/const exist but are unusable before this line

sum(3, 4);        // TypeError: sum is not a function
const sum = function (a, b) { return a + b; };
```

Three different behaviours, and the distinction is the point. A `var` declaration is hoisted
and initialised to `undefined`. A `let` or `const` declaration is hoisted but sits in the
*temporal dead zone* until its line runs, which turns a silent `undefined` into an error, and
is one of the reasons to stop writing `var`. A function *expression* assigned to a variable
follows the variable's rules, not the function declaration's, so only
[[JS Functions|the declaration form]] can be called from above.

The practical convention: define before use anyway. Hoisting is a thing to recognise when
reading someone else's code, not a thing to rely on in your own. See [[Lexical]] and
[[Variable Scope]].
